assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions — rather than one row per role/action combination
assertions.evidence: Actual table has 9 individual rows with single action values (READ, WRITE, DELETE) not value sets like {READ, WRITE, DELETE}

assertions.text: Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
assertions.evidence: Table has exactly 9 data rows: Admin read, Admin write, Admin delete, User read, User write, User cannot delete, Guest read, Guest write, Guest delete

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: Method body is single line: assertEquals(allowed, canPerform(role, action));

assertions.text: Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: First column is 'Scenario' with values like 'Admin can read', 'User cannot delete'

assertions.text: No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output — forces value set consolidation
assertions.evidence: ADMIN with READ=true, ADMIN with WRITE=true, ADMIN with DELETE=true all share role ADMIN and output true

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case
assertions.evidence: Method name 'permissionsByRoleAndAction' converts to 'Permissions By Role And Action'

assertions.text: If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express
assertions.evidence: @Description is not present; assertion passes when absent

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order
assertions.evidence: Only @TableTest annotation is present; no ordering issues

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
Scenario names describe conditions ('Admin performs any action', 'Guest reads') — not outcomes ('Allowed', 'Denied')
assertions.evidence: Scenarios: 'Admin can read', 'User cannot delete', 'Guest can read' describe conditions, not outcomes
